newsitem.title: USA: Ford July U.S. light vehicle sales rise 5.1 percent.
newsitem.headline: Ford July U.S. light vehicle sales rise 5.1 percent.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. reported a 5.1 percent increase in July U.S. car and light truck sales on Tuesday, helping to fuel a mid-summer rebound for the U.S. auto industry.

Boosted in part by a new round of incentives from Ford and General Motors Corp., U.S. industry sales during July rose 4.6 percent over a year ago to 1.35 million units. Car sales edged up 1 percent, while light truck sales were up 9.3 percent.

"It was a very strong month," said Burnham Securities auto analyst David Healy. "I think a lot of it had to do with companies throwing more incentive money at their model lines later in the month. Chrysler didn't and they were the only one with disappointing sales."

Chrysler Corp. on Friday reported a 9.3 percent drop in vehicle sales, with domestic car sales down 12.3 percent and domestic light truck sales off 7.6 percent. GM, meanwhile, said July sales rose by a surprisingly strong 6.7 percent, with domestic car sales up 2.4 percent and domestic light truck sales up 11.5 percent.

New seasonal adjustment factors had not yet been released by the U.S. Commerce Department, but based on last year's factors, sales for July came in at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of about 15.3 million units, the best rate since March and well above the 14.3 million rate in June and 14.7 million a year earlier.

PaineWebber Inc. analyst Michael Ward said he believes the market is returning to a more normal level in the third quarter after strong first-quarter sales, fuelled by payment of corporate bonuses, robbed sales from the second quarter.
"Incentive based compensation could be permanently altering the market," Ward added. "As bonuses are paid, people buy the cars, and that borrows from the second quarter."
For Ford in July, big sport utility vehicles pulled truck sales up 14.9 percent from a year ago to 200,342 units, marking the 11th consecutive monthly increase.
Ford's car sales fell 5.4 percent to 153,407 units, but executives at the No. 2 automaker said they saw some encouraging signs, including an improvement in car sales to consumers.
Sales to fleet customers, including daily rental fleets, were down 13 percent for the month, accounting for the entire car sales decline, the company said.

"Obviously, we're delighted by our continuing success in trucks," said Robert Rewey, Ford's group vice president of sales, service and marketing. "Not so obvious is that our car sales are picking up -- more than we expected. For the first time in a long time, dealers are telling us they should have ordered more cars."
The results and a continued favourable economic outlook prompted Ford to add 30,000 vehicles to its third-quarter North American production plan, split evenly between cars and trucks.

Sales of Ford's best-selling Taurus declined 11.6 percent, putting the car further behind the Toyota Camry in the race for America's best-selling car. Year-to-date sales of the Taurus were down 7.1 percent to 206,426 units, compared with 239,041 for the Camry and 194,910 for the third-place Honda Accord.
Ford's July U.S. market share rose one-tenth of a point from a year ago to 26.2 percent, while Chrysler's share fell to 14.8 percent from 17.1 percent a year ago.
GM's U.S. market share bounced back to 30.8 percent during July from a recent low of 28.4 percent in June -- within Ford's striking distance -- and 30.1 percent in July 1996.

Honda Motor Co. Ltd.'s U.S. sales during July rose an impressive 31.8 percent, enough to earn the automaker 6.5 percent of the U.S. market, up 1.3 points from a year ago. Toyota Motor Corp.'s sales rose 14.6 percent, and its market share rose seven-tenths of a point to 8.1 percent.
Nissan Motor Co. Ltd.'s sales fell 6.9 percent and Mazda Motor Corp. reported flat sales for the month.

European automakers paused in July after posting sales and share gains for several months in a row. Bayerische Motoren-Werke AG's U.S. July sales were flat, while Mercedes-Benz reported a 10.2 percent drop and Volkswagen AG reported a 14.4 percent drop. VW's Audi AG unit, however, reported a 30.1 percent increase in U.S. July sales, while AB Volvo reported a 2.8 percent gain.
Ford shares closed off 50 cents at $40.75 on the New York Stock Exchange. GM stock closed up 31 cents at $63, while Chrysler shares edged down 12.5 cents at $36.4375, also on the NYSE.
